body:
Why technical standards exist

A technical standard specifies agreed requirements that products, processes or systems must satisfy. Standards can improve safety, quality, compatibility and interoperability. Interoperability means that products or systems from different manufacturers can function together.

Mobile communication provides a useful example. Equipment manufactured by different companies must follow compatible technical specifications to communicate reliably. A shared standard helps make this possible.

Developing standards may require the use of patented inventions. This creates an important question: how can manufacturers implement a widely adopted standard when some necessary technology is protected by patents?

Meaning of a standard-essential patent

A standard-essential patent (SEP) is a patent containing at least one claim whose use is necessary to implement a particular technical standard. Essentiality depends on the patent claims and the requirements of that standard.

Not every patent relating to mobile phones or electronic devices is standard-essential. For example, a patent covering an optional decorative feature of a device would not become essential merely because the device also follows a communication standard.

Standards are commonly developed by standard-setting organisations, whose policies may address disclosure of potentially essential patents and licensing commitments. A patent owner's declaration that a patent is essential is not, by itself, conclusive proof of legal essentiality.

FRAND licensing

Some standard-setting organisations require participating patent holders to make licensing commitments on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory (FRAND) terms. Such commitments seek to balance 2 concerns: patent holders should receive suitable compensation for their inventions, while manufacturers implementing the standard should be able to obtain access on appropriate terms.

  • Fair: Licensing conditions should not be unjust or abusive.
  • Reasonable: The price and other terms should appropriately reflect the relevant rights and circumstances.
  • Non-discriminatory: Comparable licensees should not be treated unjustifiably differently in comparable circumstances.

FRAND does not necessarily mean royalty-free. It also does not require every company to pay an identical amount regardless of the nature or scope of its licence. The obligations depend on the relevant standard-setting policy, commitments made and applicable law.

Patent pools and licensing access

A patent pool is an arrangement in which multiple patent owners make specified patents available for licensing through a common mechanism. Pools may simplify access when many patents are needed to implement a technology. Their terms must nevertheless be examined for potential restrictions on competition.

Patent pools should not be confused with cross-licensing. In cross-licensing, parties grant one another rights in their respective IP. A pool creates an organised licensing arrangement for a collection of patents, potentially serving several different licensees.

Relationship between intellectual property and competition law

Patents allow a limited form of legal exclusivity. However, having a patent does not automatically prove that a company possesses a dominant position in a relevant market, and owning IP does not place every commercial practice beyond competition law.

The Competition Act, 2002 addresses anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominant position. Its Section 3(5) recognises protection for reasonable conditions necessary to protect specified intellectual property rights. This is not a general exemption for every restriction placed in an IP agreement. Section 4 deals with abuse of dominant position.

Competition concerns may arise where licensing terms unlawfully restrict market access, impose unjustified conditions or involve abusive conduct by a dominant enterprise. Each situation requires examination under the applicable legal tests. Internationally, Article 40 of the TRIPS Agreement recognises that some licensing practices or conditions may adversely affect trade and impede technology transfer, and allows members to address anti-competitive practices consistently with the Agreement.

SEP describes the relationship between a patent and a technical standard. FRAND concerns certain licensing commitments. Competition law examines the legality of market conduct. These are related but different concepts.

Prelims focus

  • SEP stands for standard-essential patent.
  • FRAND stands for fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory.
  • FRAND licensing is not necessarily royalty-free.
  • Competition Act, 2002, Section 3(5) concerns reasonable conditions needed to protect specified IP rights.
  • Competition Act, 2002, Section 4 addresses abuse of dominant position.
  • Trap: Not every patent associated with a standard is necessarily essential to implementing it.

[Sources: WIPO, Standards and Patents and Standard-Essential Patents guidance, sections on essentiality and FRAND, consulted 14 November 2026; Competition Commission of India, Antitrust guidance, consulted 14 November 2026; Competition Act, 2002, Sections 3(5) and 4; WTO, TRIPS Agreement, Article 40.]

pictures.alt: A common standard uses essential patents held by different owners; manufacturers may need licences whose terms are guided by applicable FRAND commitments.
pictures.caption: A common standard can require access to patents held by several different owners.

title: Standard-Essential Patents, FRAND Licensing and Competition

body:
Why patent rights are subject to public-interest principles

A patent provides a legally limited period of exclusive rights to encourage invention and investment. However, the law also recognises that inventions should contribute to society. This is particularly important for medicines, health technologies and other products that affect essential needs.

Patent protection can promote research by offering a possible financial return. Yet an invention may provide little immediate public benefit if it is unavailable, inadequately supplied or priced beyond the reach of those who need it. Indian patent law addresses this tension through provisions on the working of patents and compulsory licensing.

General principles under Section 83

Section 83 of the Patents Act, 1970 sets out principles relevant to the exercise of powers concerning working of patented inventions and compulsory licences. Among other matters, it recognises that patents should encourage inventions, facilitate technology transfer, contribute to technological innovation and avoid obstructing protection of public health.

The section also addresses the concern that patents should not merely enable a monopoly over the importation of patented articles. Its broader purpose is to connect patent rights with effective public benefit, including the availability of patented inventions at reasonably affordable prices.

These principles guide the statutory framework; they do not mean that every patent owner is automatically required to establish a factory in India. The legal position concerning working and imported products must be considered in the circumstances of the case and alongside India's international obligations.

Meaning of working a patent

Working a patent broadly concerns the commercial or practical exploitation of the patented invention. Relevant circumstances may include whether products or processes are being made available to the Indian market, the extent of supply and the reasons for the manner in which the invention is being exploited.

A distinction is necessary between not working an invention and not manufacturing it locally. The presence of imports does not by itself establish that an invention is unworked. Equally, importing some goods does not automatically prove that public requirements have been satisfied. The actual facts matter.

The 3 grounds under Section 84

Section 84 permits any person interested to apply to the Controller of Patents for a compulsory licence after 3 years have expired from the date the patent was granted. The application may rest on any of these alternative grounds:

  1. Unmet public requirements: The reasonable requirements of the public with respect to the patented invention have not been satisfied.
  2. Unaffordable price: The patented invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price.
  3. Non-working in India: The patented invention is not worked in the territory of India.

The grounds are alternatives, not 3 conditions that must all be proved together. However, alleging a ground does not result in an automatic licence. The Controller must examine the application and relevant statutory considerations before deciding whether relief is justified.

Reporting on patent working: Form 27

Under Section 146 of the Patents Act and Rule 131 of the Patents Rules, 2003, patentees and licensees must furnish prescribed statements concerning the working of patented inventions in Form 27.

Under the framework introduced by the Patents (Amendment) Rules, 2024, the statement is ordinarily furnished once for each period of 3 financial years, beginning with the financial year immediately following the financial year of grant. It is ordinarily due within 6 months after the end of the relevant period; on requests in Form 4, the Controller may allow extensions of up to 3 months under Rule 131(2) and up to 6 further months under Rule 138. This is the position reflected in Rule 131 as consulted on 14 November 2026; individual filing periods may involve transitional arrangements.

Form 27 is a reporting mechanism. Filing the statement does not, by itself, establish that every public-interest requirement has been met. Nor does a concern about working automatically cancel a patent.

The public-health connection

Affordable access to medicines involves several linked factors: patent rights, manufacturing capacity, distribution, health infrastructure and purchasing power. Patent law alone cannot provide hospitals or doctors, but it can influence whether manufacturers may produce protected medicines and under which conditions.

Public health therefore requires a balance between encouraging useful medical innovation and ensuring that the legal system can respond when justified public needs remain unmet.

Prelims focus

  • Section 83 states general principles concerning working and compulsory licensing.
  • Section 84 provides 3 alternative grounds: unmet public requirements, lack of a reasonably affordable price and non-working in India.
  • The ordinary Section 84 application window begins after 3 years from the date of patent grant.
  • Form 27 concerns reporting on the working of patents under Section 146 and Rule 131.
  • Under the 2024 rule change, Form 27 ordinarily covers a 3-financial-year period.
  • Trap: Importation alone does not automatically establish non-working of a patent.

[Sources: Patents Act, 1970, Sections 83, 84 and 146; Patents Rules, 2003, Rule 131, as amended in 2024, consulted 14 November 2026; Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, Form 27 FAQs dated 26 August 2024; NCERT, Social and Political Life – II, Class 7, Chapter 2, Role of the Government in Health, printed pages 18–24.]

pictures.caption: Public access to useful technologies is an important consideration in patent policy.

title: Patent Working, Affordability and the Public Interest in India

body:
Meaning of compulsory licensing

A compulsory licence is permission granted under legal authority to use a patented invention without the voluntary consent of the patent owner, subject to statutory conditions. The patent ordinarily remains in force, and the owner retains the rights that have not been displaced by the licence.

Compulsory licensing is an exception to the ordinary rule that a patent owner's consent is required for protected activities. It can help address failures of availability or affordability while retaining appropriate compensation for the owner.

The ordinary route under Section 84

After the prescribed period of 3 years from patent grant, an interested person may apply to the Controller of Patents on a statutory ground such as unmet public requirements, lack of a reasonably affordable price or non-working in India.

In examining the application, the Controller considers matters identified by law, including the nature of the invention, the applicant's ability to work it for public advantage, the applicant's capacity to undertake necessary investment and efforts to obtain a voluntary licence on reasonable terms.

Ordinarily, the applicant must first attempt to obtain permission from the patent owner on reasonable terms and conditions. Under Section 84, the relevant reasonable period is not ordinarily more than 6 months. The statute recognises exceptions to this prior-negotiation requirement for circumstances such as national emergency, extreme urgency, public non-commercial use and established anti-competitive practices.

Under the ordinary procedure, if the Controller finds a prima facie case, the application is served on the patentee and other relevant interested persons, published in the official journal, and may be opposed. A compulsory licence is therefore the outcome of a legal decision, not merely a request made by another manufacturer.

Conditions attached to a compulsory licence

Section 90 guides the terms of a licence granted under Section 84. The Controller seeks to secure reasonable royalty or remuneration, effective working of the invention and availability of the patented article at a reasonably affordable price.

Such a licence is ordinarily non-exclusive and the licensee's right is non-assignable. The licence is generally directed predominantly towards supplying the Indian market, subject to statutory exceptions. Non-exclusive means that the patent owner may continue using the invention and other permitted licensing arrangements may remain possible.

Special legal routes

ProvisionSituationImportant distinction
Section 84Ordinary compulsory licence on specified public-interest groundsApplication after 3 years from grant
Section 92National emergency, extreme urgency or public non-commercial useSpecial government-notification route
Section 92AManufacture and export of specified patented pharmaceutical products to eligible countries with insufficient or no manufacturing capacitySpecial public-health export route
Section 100Use of an invention for government purposesSeparate government-use authority

Section 92: emergency and public non-commercial use

Where the Central Government is satisfied that compulsory licences are necessary in circumstances of national emergency, extreme urgency or public non-commercial use, it may issue a notification in the Official Gazette. Following such a notification, the Controller shall grant licences on applications by interested persons under this special route. The normal 3-year waiting period applicable to Section 84 does not govern this route.

For qualifying circumstances, the Controller must dispense with the procedure specified in Section 87, while informing the patentee as soon as practicable. Public-health crises involving epidemics are expressly contemplated by the law.

Section 92A: pharmaceutical exports

Section 92A addresses manufacture and export of a patented pharmaceutical product to a country with insufficient or no manufacturing capacity for that product, where the country needs it for a public-health problem and has granted a compulsory licence or otherwise legally allowed importation from India. The Controller shall, on application, grant a licence solely for manufacture and export on terms and conditions specified and published by the Controller.

This is an important connection between Indian law and international arrangements designed to help countries that cannot manufacture the needed medicines themselves.

Section 100: government use

Section 100 separately permits use of patented inventions for government purposes by the Central Government or persons authorised in writing by it. The legal conditions and remuneration rules of government use should not be treated as identical to those of an ordinary Section 84 application.

Does a compulsory licence cancel a patent?

No. Granting a compulsory licence ordinarily leaves the patent in force. Section 85 provides a separate possible remedy: after 2 years from the order granting the first compulsory licence, the Central Government or an interested person may apply for revocation if specified problems concerning working, public requirements or affordability continue. The Controller may revoke the patent if the statutory conditions are satisfied. Revocation is not automatic.

Other exceptions are not compulsory licences

Section 107A of the Patents Act provides specified acts that are not treated as patent infringement. It includes the regulatory-use exception commonly associated with the Bolar exception, under which acts reasonably related to developing and submitting information required by a regulatory law are permitted. It also addresses importation from a person duly authorised under the law to produce and sell or distribute the patented product.

These exceptions should be distinguished from a compulsory licence. In a compulsory licence, legal authority permits specified exploitation of the patented invention. Under Section 107A, qualifying acts are treated as non-infringing by the statutory provision itself.

Indian example: Natco Pharma and Bayer

In 2012, India granted a compulsory licence to Natco Pharma relating to Bayer's patented cancer medicine sorafenib tosylate, marketed as Nexavar. The decision is an important Indian example of the use of Section 84 in a public-interest context. It does not establish that every patented medicine with a high price must automatically be compulsorily licensed.

Prelims focus

  • Section 84 is the ordinary compulsory-licensing route; the waiting period is 3 years from patent grant.
  • Prior efforts to obtain a voluntary licence are ordinarily relevant; the reasonable period is not ordinarily more than 6 months.
  • Section 90 ordinarily provides for a non-exclusive, non-assignable licence and reasonable remuneration.
  • Section 92 concerns government-notified emergency, extreme urgency or public non-commercial use.
  • Section 92A concerns specified pharmaceutical exports; Section 100 concerns government use.
  • Section 85 allows an application for possible revocation 2 years after the first compulsory-licence order.
  • Trap: Compulsory licensing is not the same as immediate revocation of the patent.

[Sources: Patents Act, 1970, Sections 84, 85, 87, 90, 92, 92A, 100 and 107A, consulted 14 November 2026; Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, Manual of Patent Office Practice and Procedure, section on compulsory licences; Government of India, Press Information Bureau, statement on compulsory licensing dated 31 December 2018; WTO, TRIPS and Public Health, Compulsory Licensing of Pharmaceuticals FAQ, consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Section 84 requires a 3-year wait; Section 92 uses government notification. A revocation application may follow after 2 years if specified failures persist.
pictures.caption: Ordinary compulsory licensing and special urgent licensing follow different paths.

title: Compulsory Licensing in India: Procedure, Exceptions and Remedies
